newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council issues mild statement on Iraqi flight.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council issues mild statement on Iraqi flight.

text.p: The Security Council, in a setback for the United States, issued a mild statement on Wednesday that refrained from calling a recent Iraqi pilgrim flight to Saudi Arabia a breach of Gulf war sanctions.

The statement read out by the president, the result of several days of tortuous negotiations, said Iraq proceeded with the flight "without specific consultation" with the council's Iraqi sanctions committee.
"Such consultation would have allowed the committee to consider the matter and to determine whether the flight required committee approval under the relevant resolutions."

Several council members, including China, were reported to have said during the consultations that they did not believe Iraq had violated sanctions in force since shortly after its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The issuing of a formal statement by the council president requires the consensus of all 15 members.

The U.N. legal counsel, Hans Corell of Sweden, was reported to have told the sanctions committee last week that sanctions affecting flights by Iraqi aircraft were not as clear-cut as those banning flights by Libya because of its involvement in the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland.
But he added that, based on past committee practice, he believed the Iraqi flight required the committee's authorisation.

American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson told reporters on April 9 that the flight earlier that day, which took 104 pilgrims from Baghdad to Jeddah, was "an outright violation of sanctions" and that he was seeking a strong council statement to that effect.

After Wednesday's statement was issued at a brief council meeting, Richardson said: "The United States still believes that the unauthorised flight by Iraq was a violation of Security Council resolutions. We welcome the presidential statement. Most of the members agree with us and recognise that it is based on the consensus of all members.
"We firmly believe that it is up to the sanctions committee to determine what is permissible under the resolutions, and not Iraq," he said.

Richardson said the statement that was issued "suits our purposes and our policy," adding that he and the U.S. government "have the utmost respect for the right of all Moslems to participate in the haj."

The statement noted that Iraq had asked the sanctions committee in February to release $50 million from frozen Iraqi assets in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates to cover pilgrimage costs and requested the committee's agreement for Iraqi Airways to fly the pilgrims to Jeddah.

The statement said the committee had replied in March that it would be in a better position to consider the release of the frozen Iraqi funds if a request were submitted by a country willing to release such funds for that purpose.

"The government of Iraq proceeded with this particular flight without specific consultation with the committee," said the statement, which also underlined the council's "respect for the obligation of Moslems to perform the haj pilgrimage."
